panel: notebook: Lab, step 3 (macOS and Linux bullet)
what: The lab says a Linux locale has to be installed for LC_ALL to work, and that Node otherwise falls back to en-US. That is false, and the chapter's own capture disproves it: the capture machine has only C, C.utf8, POSIX and en_US.utf8 installed, yet panel 25's LC_ALL=de_DE.UTF-8 and LC_ALL=hi_IN.UTF-8 runs printed de-DE and hi-IN. Node's ICU reads the LC_ALL variable directly.
evidence: Page: "On Linux the locale must be installed ( locale -a lists them); if it isn't, Node falls back to en-US ." `locale -a` on the capture machine: C, C.utf8, POSIX, en_US.utf8. data/js-ch23.json locale_default.js steps 2 and 3 print `1.234.567,891` / `de-DE` and `12,34,567.891` / `hi-IN`. Scratch runs with Node 26.13.0: LC_ALL=fr_CA.UTF-8 gives fr-CA, and LC_ALL=zz_QQ.UTF-8 gives zz-QQ (neither locale is installed).
fix: Replace the sentence with: "Node reads LC_ALL itself, so this works even for locales your system hasn't installed (this book's de_DE and hi_IN runs were made that way). Other programs on your system, like `date`, may still complain about a missing locale."

what: The lab says Ctrl + C can't stop a stuck regex in the Node REPL until it finishes. That's wrong: the REPL interrupts a catastrophic regex straight away with ERR_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_INTERRUPTED.
evidence: Page: "in the REPL, a stuck regex can't be stopped by Ctrl + C until it finishes. Close the terminal tab if it happens." Scratch test: a real Node 26.13.0 REPL in a pty, evaluating /^(a+)+$/.test("a".repeat(36)+"!"). Ctrl+C after 1.5 s printed `code: 'ERR_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_INTERRUPTED'` and a fresh `>` prompt, and `1+1` then printed 2. The same happens with vm.runInThisContext(..., {breakOnSigint: true}): "Script execution was interrupted by `SIGINT`" after 1015 ms.
fix: Replace the bullet with: "Don't run catastrophic patterns on purpose. If one gets stuck in the REPL, Ctrl + C interrupts it. In a script started with node file.js, Ctrl + C ends the whole program."

what: The page says promisify doesn't fit setTimeout because its callback comes first. In Node, util.promisify(setTimeout) does work: setTimeout carries a util.promisify.custom version, and Node's docs show this exact use.
evidence: Page: "setTimeout is a callback function too, but its callback comes first, so promisify doesn't fit." Scratch run on Node 26.13.0: `promisify(setTimeout)(10, "promisified setTimeout works").then(console.log)` printed `promisified setTimeout works`.
fix: Reword to: "setTimeout takes its callback first, so the usual error-first recipe doesn't apply. (Node special-cases it, so promisify(setTimeout) works, but wrapping it yourself takes one line and works everywhere, browsers included.)"

what: The lab says everything except using, DisposableStack, Error.isError and Promise.try works from Node 18. But with_resolvers.js (panel 24) uses Promise.withResolvers, which only arrived in Node 22.
evidence: Page: "using , DisposableStack , Error.isError and Promise.try need a recent Node (26 has them all, 22 has none); everything else works from Node 18." with_resolvers.js line 1 calls `Promise.withResolvers()`. MDN gives its Baseline date as March 2024 (Chrome 119, V8 11.9). Node 20 ships V8 11.3, and Node 22.0 was the first release with V8 12.
fix: Change to "…everything else works from Node 22 (Promise.withResolvers needs 22; the rest works from Node 18)."

what: The feature-age list dates regex literals, test, exec, match, replace and search to "the first editions (1997–1999)" and lists lazy quantifiers and lookahead separately as ES3. Regular expressions as a whole first arrived in ES3 (1999); ES1 and ES2 had no RegExp.
evidence: Page: "regex literals, test , exec , match , replace , split and search are from the first editions (1997–1999); lazy quantifiers and lookahead from ES3 (1999)".
fix: Change to "split (with a string) is from ES1 (1997); regular expressions themselves (literals, test, exec, match, replace, search, regex split, lazy quantifiers and lookahead) arrived in ES3 (1999)".

panel: notebook: Under the hood, "Who owns lastIndex"
what: The note says only direct calls to test and exec leak lastIndex. A sticky regex without g also leaks it through match and replace.
evidence: Page: "…so only direct calls to test and exec leak state between uses." Scratch run, Node 26.13.0: `const r=/a/y; "ab".match(r)` leaves r.lastIndex at 1, a second identical match returns null, and `"ab".replace(/a/y, "x")` leaves lastIndex at 1.
fix: Append: "…(and match or replace with a sticky regex that has no g, which read and move lastIndex too)."

what: The note says BigInt() reads a string "as BigInt code". It doesn't: BigInt code ends in n, and BigInt("10n") is a SyntaxError. The string must be a plain whole-number literal.
evidence: m-big note: "From text, the machine reads the string as BigInt code, and 1.5 isn't valid BigInt syntax". Scratch run, Node 26.13.0: BigInt("10n") throws "Cannot convert 10n to a BigInt".
fix: Change to "From text, the machine accepts only whole-number digits (no decimal point, and no n), so \"1.5\" is a SyntaxError."

what: The note says 1000.1 + 1000.2 is as close to 2000.3 as the ruler allows. It isn't: it lands one mark above the mark where 2000.3 is stored, which is why line 7 prints 2000.3000000000002 and not 2000.3.
evidence: Page: "The plain test says false , even though the sum is as close as the ruler allows." epsilon.js line 7 prints 2000.3000000000002. The difference is 2.27e-13, one gap (2^-42) near 2000.
fix: Change to "…even though the sum is only one mark away."

what: Kit says the date shows as the 6th to everyone west of London. The rule is "clocks behind UTC": Iceland, Portugal and Ireland are west of London and still show the 7th in November. Boss 6 already says it correctly ("west of UTC").
evidence: Page: "…will show the 6th to everyone west of London." ex-b6-m: "The date shifts to the 6th for every visitor west of UTC".
fix: Change to "…to everyone whose clock is behind UTC (the Americas, for example)."
